title: Tax capital gains like income: 20%, 40% and 45%
headline: CenTax’s package on today’s baseline, after behaviour: £19.7bn a year.
description: The reported front-runner for this Budget is to charge capital gains at income tax rates, phased in. The Centre for the Analysis of Taxation costs a package that does that: rates of 20%, 40% and 45%, an investment allowance so that only real returns above a normal rate are taxed, the write-off of gains at death removed, a charge on people who leave the country, Business Asset Disposal Relief and Investors’ Relief abolished and losses reformed. In September 2026 it re-costed the package on the OBR’s current forecast, after the October 2024 rate rise and the move of carried interest into income tax: a 62% rise in CGT revenue, down from the 88% it estimated in 2024, but £19.7 billion in 2029-30 because the OBR now expects twice the CGT it did then. That is CenTax’s central estimate after behavioural responses, held flat in cash here; most of it comes from people with large gains, and part of it arrives as income tax.

baselinePolicy.text: Capital gains are taxed at 18% and 24% (residential property and carried interest apart), with gains written off at death, no charge on leaving the country, and Business Asset Disposal Relief at 18% from April 2026. CGT receipts are forecast at £32.0bn in 2029-30.
alreadyIncludes: The October 2024 rise in the main rates to 18% and 24% and the BADR and Investors’ Relief changes (Autumn Budget 2024, Table 5.1 line 27).

terms.label: CenTax’s central estimate for its package in 2029-30 on the OBR’s current baseline, after behavioural responses

source.quote: It equates to £19.7 billion of additional revenue in 2030 given the current Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) baseline forecast of £32 billion for CGT

rawSource.note: CenTax’s September 2026 figure for the whole package, on the OBR’s March 2026 forecast for capital gains tax, held flat in cash from the start year. It supersedes the 2024 estimate of £14 billion, which was costed from the old 10% and 20% rates and needed the 2024 rise netting off; this one does not. Effects before the start year are not applied.

caveats: A package, not a rate change. CenTax’s £19.7 billion assumes an investment allowance, the death write-off removed, a charge on leavers, BADR and Investors’ Relief abolished and losses reformed. Rates alone would raise far less: HMRC’s own reckoner scores a ten-point rise in the higher rate as losing money, and CenTax advises against equalising rates without the base reforms.

A central estimate after behaviour, held flat in cash: CenTax says the base reforms close the usual escape routes (holding to death, leaving the country), so the response is smaller than to a bare rate rise; the 2024 report’s worst case was two thirds of its central figure. Forestalling would cut the first years.

Seventy per cent of the revenue comes from people in the top 0.1% by five-year remuneration; a substantial share arrives as income tax rather than CGT as people stop turning income into gains. Nobody has certified any of it.

considerations.text: CenTax’s figure already allows for people realising fewer gains, holding assets longer and leaving; without the charge on leavers it says the migration response could push revenue below its worst case. The OBR would take its own view of all of that.

sources.quote: Our estimate accounts for behavioural responses, but these are uncertain and sensitive to policy design

considerations.text: Capital gains are concentrated among a small number of people with large gains, and the package taxes them at their income tax rate; the investment allowance means smaller, ordinary returns would pay less than today.

interactions.text: The package already sets the rates at 20%, 40% and 45%; a further rise on top of it is not what CenTax costed.
The package already takes the lower rate to 20%; stacking a rise here double counts.
CenTax’s package already removes the write-off at death; that card’s £4bn would be counted twice.
CenTax’s package already charges people who leave; that card’s £0.5bn would be counted twice.
Reversing the 2024 rise while aligning rates is contradictory: the £2.5bn netted off here would come back.
The package abolishes Business Asset Disposal Relief; moving its rate as well adds nothing CenTax costed.
